meeting_header:
Date: 2026-11-10 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 47 min
Location: Zoom | Recording: enabled
Redwood: Avery Patel (AE), Jamal Rivera (SE)
Pegasus AI: Rina Kapoor (Head of ML), Mark D'Souza (Infra Lead), Sofia Li (Security), Tom Nguyen (Product)
summary: Intro discovery focused on dedicated capacity needs: isolation requirements, burst model for traffic spikes, expected concurrency/latency SLAs, and roadmap for a short pilot. Customer leaning toward Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) with a private VPC option but wants clearer failover and cost tradeoffs.
topics: Burst strategy: hot pool, pre-warm, fallback
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — quick intros from our side, I'm Avery, AE for Redwood. Jamal's our SE.
[00:06] Rina: Hey, I'm Rina, lead for ML at Pegasus. Thanks. Mark here — infra. Sofia security, and Tom product.
[00:14] Jamal: Great, high level goal for today is to understand your capacity profile and isolation needs so we can map the right Dedicated plan, plus burst behavior — wanna hear current patterns.
[00:24] Rina: Sure. We're replacing an internal serving layer, we currently run models on a mix of preemptible VMs and some GKE nodes. It's been okay but spikes crush us and tail latency is bad. We are evaluating Redwood Hosted versus Dedicated and also possibility of a private VPC. Primary concerns: predictability, data isolation, and cost when traffic surges.
[00:43] Avery: Understood. Can you give ballpark traffic and concurrency?
[00:47] Mark: On a typical day it's around 150 QPS at peak, but we have several batch weekends that can jump to 1,800 QPS for short periods — like 5-20 minutes. Concurrency for real-time calls is usually 400 concurrent streams with avg seq length ~260 tokens.
[01:05] Jamal: Ok that helps. Two immediate levers: reserved Dedicated pools for predictable baseline throughput, and a burst strategy — either hot pre-warm pools we keep idle or on-demand burst to lower-tier instances. Are you prioritizing latency or cost during the spike?
[01:20] Rina: Latency's primary, user-facing product, so 95th under 300ms is our target. We can tolerate some scale-to-cost during spikes but not if it kills 95th.
[01:31] Sofia: Also we need tenant isolation for some regulated clients — logs and models can't leave our VPC, and keys must be customer-managed. SOC 2 and encryption at rest are must-haves.
[01:42] Avery: Good — Redwood Dedicated with Private control plane can do VPC peering and customer KMS / HSM integrations. Jamal, do you want to explain isolation options?
[01:50] Jamal: Sure. We offer three deployment patterns: shared-hosted (multi-tenant), dedicated-reserved pools (your GPUs isolated to your tenant), and private deployment (control plane in your VPC, optional on-prem). For regulated tenants you'd pick either dedicated with VPC peering plus strict network rules, or full Private for air-gapped needs. Note: "Redwood Dedicate" — sorry, Dedicated — includes tenant-level auditing and RBAC.
[02:12] Tom: What about noisy neighbor risk within Dedicated?
[02:15] Jamal: With reserved pools, you're the only tenant on those nodes so noisy neighbors are eliminated. The remaining question is how you want to handle burst: keep a small hot pool ready (pre-warmed GPUs), or autoscale into shared capacity with fallback models that are cheaper/quantized.
[02:29] Rina: We like the hot pool idea but cost is a concern. How do you size a hot pool?
[02:33] Jamal: We typically look at spike shape and SLO. You gave short spikes of 5-20 minutes to 1,800 QPS. For that we'd recommend a baseline reserved pool sized for median peak (~200 QPS) plus a hot pool sized to absorb the typical 95th spike headroom, with automatic pre-warm policy. You can combine with a fallback policy where, if hot pool threshold exceeded, we route to lower-cost quantized model that can handle more concurrency but slightly worse quality.
[02:55] Mark: That fallback sounds risky for product team. How transparent is it?
[02:59] Jamal: You can define per-route policies: first choice Dedicated high-accuracy model, fallback to quantized variant with explicit tags, and Redwood Console will flag rollback. You can also set canary percentages during rollouts.
[03:10] Rina: What's the cold-start time for a new GPU slot?
[03:13] Jamal: Cold start varies by model and infra. For large Llama-style models it can be 30–90s to load if not pre-warmed due to KV cache, kernel priming. Pre-warmed hot pool eliminates that. We also do continuous batching so per-token latency is stable once warmed.
[03:27] Sofia: For compliance, can pre-warmed instances sit inside our VPC and have customer-managed keys?
[03:32] Jamal: Yes, with Private or Dedicated + VPC peering + KMS integration. The keys can be customer-managed; we do audit logs and show token-level traces as needed. We'll share SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[03:45] Tom: Cost model — what's the unit economics? How do we pay for hot pool vs reserved?
[03:49] Avery: Reserved pool is committed monthly or annual pricing; hot pool can be configured as reserved (lower rate) or on-demand burst (higher rate). We'll send a worksheet showing per-GPU reserved vs burst-on-demand and an example for your expected spike profile.
[04:03] Rina: Can we test this with a short pilot? Like provision a 3-GPU reserved pool and run a synthetic that mimics weekend hops?
[04:09] Jamal: Absolutely. Typical pilot: 2–4 week window, we provision a small reserved pool, run your traffic patterns, and measure latency/throughput. We can also do a hybrid: dedicated baseline + hot pool for spikes, and we run the benchmark with both enabled.
[04:21] Mark: Network egress during spike — we need predictable bandwidth. How does Redwood handle networking inside VPC peering?
[04:28] Jamal: We support VPC peering and private endpoints. Egress is across peered network and you manage routing. For very high throughput we advise colocated regions to reduce cross-region egress. We'll include network diagrams in the docs.
[04:39] Rina: Model versioning and rollouts — we need canary and rollback.
[04:43] Jamal: Redwood Console supports model pinning, canary percentages, automatic rollback based on quality/regression alerts (you can supply eval prompt sets). This is standard.
[04:52] Sofia: Audit trails — are token-level logs stored? For some clients we need to retain logs for 90 days and have them available for compliance checks.
[04:58] Jamal: Yes, we have configurable retention. For Private deployments you control retention windows; for hosted Dedicated we can negotiate extended retention in enterprise plans. Logs are encrypted and can be pushed to your S3 or SIEM.
[05:07] Tom: Any prerequisites on our side for private control plane?
[05:10] Jamal: Network access and an IP allowlist, a KMS key for encryption, and a small set of bootstrap credentials. We'll provide a VPC onboarding checklist.
[05:17] Rina: How does failover look if your region runs out of capacity during a large spike?
[05:22] Jamal: We support policy-based routing: first prefer your dedicated pool, then prefer regional compatible capacity, then fallback to hosted multi-tenant instances or quantized models. You can also configure cross-region failover if latency tradeoff is acceptable. Important: with reserved Dedicated, we prioritize your capacity but extreme cloud-wide shortages can still trigger fallback.
[05:40] Mark: For billing transparency, can we get token-level cost breakdowns?
[05:43] Avery: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdown per route and model. We'll include sample reports.
[05:49] Rina: A couple of questions from product: sequence lengths — we sometimes have unusually long contexts (up to 2,400 tokens) for a few call types. How does that change sizing?
[05:59] Jamal: Long seq lengths increase memory and reduce per-GPU concurrency since KV cache scales. For a 2.4k window you'd expect lower concurrent connections per GPU. We'll run sizing with your real distribution — please send histograms and percentiles.
[06:12] Tom: On security, we need SAML SSO + RBAC for devs, and ability to restrict model publishing to a handful of users.
[06:19] Jamal: Supported — SSO + SCIM sync and fine-grained RBAC. Model publishing can be gated.
[06:24] Sofia: Any existing customers with similar compliance needs?
[06:27] Avery: Yes — a healthcare SaaS and a fintech customer run Dedicated + Private with HSMs. We'll share high-level diagrams and redacted reference checklist.
[06:35] Rina: Ok, let's talk numbers: For a 3-slot pool (NVIDIA A100 equivalents), what's typical throughput?
[06:41] Jamal: Depends on model family and quantization. For a medium Llama 2 variant: one A100-ish slot might do ~80–120 simultaneous low-latency requests with batching; so 3 slots could handle a few hundred concurrent low-latency requests, but if many are long sequences that's lower. We'll run the pilot to get exact.
[06:57] Mark: What about pre-warm cost if we keep a 2-slot hot pool active 24/7?
[07:02] Avery: Pre-warm reserved pricing is lower than on-demand but still billed. We'll model scenarios in the worksheet: reserved baseline + reserved hotpool vs reserved baseline + on-demand hotpool.
[07:13] Tom: Are there knobs for batching? We have clients with lots of small requests.
[07:17] Jamal: Yes, continuous batching and adaptive batch sizes are part of the runtime. You can tune max latency vs batching window. For lots of small requests, batching reduces unit token cost significantly.
[07:27] Rina: I heard some runtimes struggle with KV cache in multi-model scenarios. If we do canary rollouts with two model versions, does KV cache thrash?
[07:35] Jamal: The runtime isolates KV caches per model instance; if you running two large variants on same node you'll see memory pressure. For canaries we often spin up separate pre-warmed instances to avoid cache thrash.
[07:45] Sofia: On encryption keys — do you support rotation and annual key audits?
[07:48] Jamal: Yes, rotation supported via your KMS and we expose audit logs for key ops.
[07:53] Mark: Who do we talk to internally for a security deep dive?
[07:56] Avery: I'll loop in our Security Solutions lead, Priya Nair, for a dedicated session.
[08:00] Rina: Ok, next steps?
[08:03] Avery: We'll send a pricing + burst worksheet, SOC2 and KMS docs, and a VPC checklist. You send us traffic histograms and latency SLOs and we'll schedule a benchmark week of Nov 22.
[08:13] Tom: Sounds good.
[08:15] Sofia: Quick question — do you have pre-built quantized model images?
[08:19] Jamal: Yes, we maintain quantized variants for common families; if you need custom quant, we can help with quantization and quality evals during pilot.
[08:26] Rina: One more: For peak weekend jobs (1,800 QPS) — would you recommend short-term scaling or throttling? We can't drop client requests.
[08:34] Jamal: If dropping is not acceptable we recommend a multi-pronged approach: larger hot pool for weekend windows, cross-region failover, and an SLA agreement for burst guarantees. Also consider pre-queueing some heavy jobs to batch them outside synchronous user flows.
[08:48] Mark: Ok we have enough to estimate. We'll share the histograms and a list of regulated tenants.
[08:54] Avery: Great — we'll follow up with docs and the pricing workbook. Thanks all.
[08:58] Rina: Thank you.
[09:00] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-hearings; references shared: capacity-workbook.xlsx, SOC2-summary.pdf, VPC-onboarding-checklist.md.
